transcript.text: I've been undercharging for years. I set
my prices when I was just starting out
and had zero experience and I never
raised them. I want to raise my rates by
40% but I'm terrified I'll lose half my
clients who have been with me from the
start and I feel guilty about pricing
them out. How do you actually pull the
trigger on a big price increase?
>> Okay, so first off, it depends on how
many customers you have. If you have
just a handful that you can count, this
would be a conversation.
Um, if it's, you know, hundreds of
customers, then it might be something
that I would send as an email or uh, an
actual like paper mail. Step one, thank
them for being a customer and remind
them of the value that you've delivered
them over time. That's the first part of
the letter, talking two, three
sentences. The next paragraph, you say,
"I promised you this and I promised you
this and I promised you this and I said
I was going to be the best and for that
reason, in service of this ideal and of
my promise to you, I have to keep
investing in the business and so because
of that, I have to raise these prices."
And when I say have to, we're going to
say,
"Prices have gone up." And so what this
does is it gives you also a moral high
ground from a from an argumentation
perspective because you're saying,
"Wait, if you're arguing against this,
are you saying that I should break my
promise to you? Are you saying that I
should not be a man of my word or a
woman of my word? That I should have
inferior service?" I don't think that's
fair to you and I don't think that's
fair to the other customers. That being
said, next paragraph,
"As
a thank you for being a loyal customer,
you are going to have a six-month
discount or three-month discount that
I'm automatically going to apply to your
account for this next three or six
months, whatever it is,
uh, before it comes into play as a thank
you to you." Now, what we're going to be
doing with this money is investment
number one, investment number two,
investment number three, we're going to
improve our service, whatever your
things are, and say, "Again, thank you
so much." Um, and then PS, if you're
B2C, say like if this is going to
prevent you from buying groceries or
paying your mortgage, um, please let me
know and we'll figure something out. And
if you're B2B, say, "Hey, um, if this is
going to materially damage your
business, uh, please reach out to me.
I'm sure we can figure something out."
And so that's how I would do the price
raise.
